title: OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange
subtitle: One service trades a user's token for a narrower, delegated token to call the next service in the chain — with an act claim that keeps the acting party auditable (RFC 8693).

steps.label: Request that fans out to service B
steps.lede: Service A already holds the user's access token. To fulfil the request it must call service B on the user's behalf — but it should present a token scoped to B, not the user's full token.
steps.devtools: The exchange that follows is a back-channel, service-to-service call. None of it appears in the browser Network tab — watch service A's egress logs or the STS access logs.

steps.label: POST /token (token-exchange grant)
steps.lede: Service A posts the user's token as subject_token and asks the Security Token Service to mint a token for a narrower audience and scope. It authenticates with its own client credentials.
steps.devtools: URL-decode the form body. The Basic value decodes to svc-a:svc-a-s3cr3t. Key params: subject_token (who the new token represents), audience and scope — these should narrow, never widen, the downstream reach.

steps.label: Validate + mint delegated token
steps.lede: The STS validates the subject_token, checks its may_act policy permits service A to act for the user, then mints a delegated token: same subject (the user), narrowed aud and scope, plus an act claim naming service A.
steps.devtools: No network event. The may_act check is the authorization gate: if the subject token's policy does not list service A as a permitted actor, the exchange is denied with 400 invalid_request.

steps.label: 200 issued delegated token
steps.lede: The STS returns the exchanged token. issued_token_type reports what was actually minted (it may differ from what was requested). expires_in is short — 5 minutes here.

jwt.title: Decoded access_token (at+jwt)
payload: The USER — unchanged by the exchange
ACTOR chain — service A is acting for the user

steps.devtools: The single most important claim to read is act. Its presence ({"sub":"svc-a"}) means this is delegation: downstream can see who is acting. An impersonation token would be identical minus the act claim — the actor invisible. Chains nest: "act":{"sub":"svc-b","act":{"sub":"svc-a"}}, read outermost-first.

steps.label: Call service B with the delegated token
steps.lede: Service A calls service B presenting the exchanged token as a Bearer credential. This hop is typically service-to-service as well.
steps.devtools: Decode the Bearer token and confirm service B sees sub=user and act.sub=svc-a, and enforces the narrowed read:orders scope against itself. The user is present, the acting service is auditable.

steps.label: Denied — may_act does not permit this actor
steps.lede: If the exchange supplies an actor_token whose identity is not listed in the subject token's may_act, the STS refuses to mint a delegated token.
steps.devtools: The policy check failed: the subject token's may_act did not authorize the requested actor (e.g. service X). Delegation is preferred over impersonation precisely because this authority is explicit and, in the issued token, auditable via act.
